Pulmonary hypertension Pulmonary hypertension is a disorder in which there is an increase in pulmonary vascular resistance, leading to an increase in pulmonary arterial pressure. Mean pulmonary artery pressure in a resting individual at sea level is nor- mally about 15 mmHg; pulmonary hypertension is usually defined as a pressure above 25 mmHg at rest, or above 30 mmHg during exercise. Pressures will be correspond- ingly higher at higher altitudes. Pulmonary hypertension has been classified in a number of ways and the terminology used has changed as the un- derlying pathophysiology has become clearer. The most common classification used has been to divide pulmonary hypertension into primary and secondary forms, depend- ing on the absence or presence of an underlying cause. However, this classification has little meaning in terms of the pathophysiology or treatment and guidelines1,2 now recommend against the use of these terms. Pulmonary arterial hypertension is the preferred term where the in- creased pressure is due to a disorder of the pulmonary arteries themselves. This includes both idiopathic and fa- milial forms (previously classified as primary pulmonary hypertension), as well as forms that were previously clas- sified as secondary, including those associated with con- nective tissue disorders, infections, drugs and toxins, and a number of other disorders. The discussion that follows re- lates to the management of these forms. Other types are classified into groups covering pulmonary hypertension associated with cardiac, pulmonary, thromboembolic, or other disorders, for which management primarily involves treatment of the underlying disease. Pulmonary arterial hypertension3-8 is a progressive dis- ease with a high mortality rate, and patients appear to be prone to sudden death.
